title: Who preserves a place's story?
essentialQuestion: How do records made while people care for an old place help others learn about it later, and what can those records not tell us?
learningGoal: Explain the difference between Borobudur's ancient building and its modern conservation, and write a dated caption for a conservation photo.

warmUp.question: If you were repairing a very old building, what would you want to write down?

evidence.question: Which source tells you about the ancient monument? Which ones tell you about the work done in the 1970s?

sources.caption: Source 1: UNESCO's World Heritage description of the Borobudur Temple Compounds (a modern heritage account)
details: Written by UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, for the World Heritage List.
It says Borobudur was built in the 700s and 800s, in the Kedu Valley in Central Java, Indonesia.
It describes stone terraces, walls carved with pictures, and 72 small stupas, each with a statue of the Buddha.
It says the monument was restored with UNESCO's help, most recently from 1973 to 1983, using its original stones.
Limit: it is a modern account. It is not a record left by the people who built Borobudur.

sources.caption: Source 2: The Borobudur Conservation Archives (records made from 1973 to 1983)
details: Made by the restoration project, which the Government of Indonesia and UNESCO carried out with help from other countries.
Kept today by the Borobudur Conservation Office in Indonesia.
The archive's record at UNESCO lists 71,851 sheets of photos, 6,043 sheets of as-built drawings and maps, films and 425 project documents.
UNESCO's Memory of the World programme recognised the archive in 2017.
Limit: it records the modern work. It cannot tell us what the first builders planned.

sources.caption: Source 3: A photo of conservation work at Borobudur, taken in 1976 by Gerard Bolla for UNESCO
details: Kept in UNESCO's archives and shared on Wikimedia Commons by UNESCO.
It shows the upper levels of the stone monument, with metal scaffolding along one side and rows of small stupas below a large one at the top.

A typed note on the back of the print, written by UNESCO, says the temple was slowly falling apart, and that in October 1972 UNESCO's board approved an agreement with Indonesia's government to save it.
Limit: it shows one moment in 1976. It cannot show why each repair was chosen.

events.text: People build Borobudur in Central Java.
A large restoration project takes place, with Indonesia and UNESCO working together.
Gerard Bolla photographs the conservation work for UNESCO.
UNESCO's Memory of the World programme recognises the conservation archive.

sections.heading: Two times at one place
sections.text: Borobudur is a Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia. It was built in the 700s and 800s. It has stone terraces, walls carved with pictures, and 72 small stupas, or bell-shaped towers. Each stupa holds a statue of the Buddha. UNESCO explains that its levels follow a Buddhist idea of the universe. Many centuries later, people faced a new question: how should it be conserved? A large restoration ran from 1973 to 1983. Indonesia and UNESCO did the work, with help from other countries. The people who restored Borobudur did not build it. It helps to keep these two times apart.
sections.simpler: Borobudur is a Buddhist temple on the island of Java. People built it more than 1,000 years ago. It has stone steps and walls with carved pictures. At the top are 72 small stone towers. Each one holds a statue of the Buddha. From 1973 to 1983, a big team fixed it. This careful work is called conservation. Indonesia and UNESCO did it together. The team did not build the temple.

sections.heading: An archive made during work
sections.text: An archive is a set of records kept so people can study them later. During the restoration, the team took photos, made drawings and films, and wrote reports. An office at Borobudur keeps them today. Its list counts 71,851 sheets of photos and 6,043 sheets of as-built drawings and maps. An as-built drawing shows what workers found and recorded during the work. It is not a plan from the first builders. A later conservator can compare a photo with a drawing and ask why a repair was made. In 2017, UNESCO gave the archive recognition. That date is about the records, not the monument.
sections.simpler: An archive is a set of records. People keep them to look at later. During the work, the team took photos. They made drawings and wrote notes. There are 71,851 sheets of photos. There are 6,043 sheets of as-built drawings. An as-built drawing shows what the workers found. Later, people can look at a photo and a drawing. They can ask why a part was fixed. In 2017, UNESCO gave the archive recognition. That date is about the records.

sections.heading: A photograph from 1976
sections.text: The second picture is a photo taken in 1976 by Gerard Bolla for UNESCO. It records a moment of modern conservation work. Look at what is in the photo, then ask what is outside it. A photo cannot tell us what the first builders planned, or why each repair was chosen. It cannot tell us what Borobudur means to every visitor and worshipper. People can add to the record. In 2019, a show of photos by Suparno opened near Borobudur. He worked at the Borobudur office and was trained to photograph the repairs. His memories can answer questions one photo leaves open.
sections.simpler: The second picture is a photo from 1976. Gerard Bolla took it for UNESCO. It shows the work to fix the temple. It does not show the first builders. The photo cannot show what they planned. It cannot show what the place means to each person who comes. In 2019, there was a show of photos by Suparno. He worked at Borobudur and took photos of the work. People like him can tell us more.

glossary.definition: Careful work to protect a place or object so it lasts.
glossary.example: Conservation work at Borobudur ran from 1973 to 1983.

glossary.definition: A set of records kept safely so people can study them later.
glossary.example: The Borobudur archive holds photos, drawings, films and reports.

glossary.definition: A drawing of a building as workers found and recorded it.
glossary.example: An as-built drawing shows a wall as the team recorded it during the repairs.

glossary.definition: When a group says, at a later time, that something is important.
glossary.example: The archive got UNESCO recognition in 2017, long after the repairs ended.

options.feedback: Not quite. Borobudur was built in the 700s and 800s. Check the date of the photo in the third part of the reading.

options.text: The archive being honoured by UNESCO

options.text: Modern conservation work on the monument
options.feedback: Yes. The photo records repair work in 1976, more than 1,000 years after Borobudur was built.

checks.question: Which of these is kept in the Borobudur conservation archive?

options.feedback: Yes. The archive holds as-built drawings, photos, films and reports from the 1973 to 1983 work.

options.text: Letters written by the first builders
options.feedback: Not quite. The archive was made during the modern repairs. Look at the second part of the reading.

options.text: Photos taken while it was first built
options.feedback: Not quite. Cameras did not exist in the 700s and 800s. Look at the dates in the reading.

write.prompt: Write a two-sentence caption for the 1976 photo that says who took it, when, and what it shows. Then write two questions the photo cannot answer.
sentenceStarters: This photo was taken in ... by ...
One question the photo cannot answer is ...
selfCheck: I said who took the photo and when.
I said what the photo shows.
I wrote two questions the photo cannot answer.
write.example: This photo was taken in 1976 by Gerard Bolla for UNESCO. It shows repair work at Borobudur, not the first builders. It does not show the people who built it in the 700s and 800s. One question the photo cannot answer is how the first builders planned each level. Another question is why the team chose each repair. A drawing or a report from the archive might help.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, decide whose views should count when people care for Borobudur: conservators, people who live nearby, people who come to worship, or visitors. Give one reason for each group you choose.
speak.independentTask: Write a short note that names two groups who should have a say in caring for Borobudur, with one reason for each.

watch.title: Borobudur Temple Compounds (UNESCO/NHK)
watch.why: A short UNESCO and NHK film about the ancient monument itself, which helps learners keep the monument apart from its modern conservation.
watch.beforeQuestion: Do you think a short film about Borobudur will be about the old monument, the 1970s repairs, or both?
watch.afterQuestion: Listen for when the film says Borobudur was built. Write down the centuries it gives.
watch.summary: This short film was made by NHK, a broadcaster from Japan, with UNESCO. It is about the ancient monument and what it may mean. Borobudur stands in Central Java, in Indonesia. It was built in the 700s and 800s. It has stone terraces, and its walls are covered with carved pictures. The film explains that the levels may follow a Buddhist idea of the universe. At the top there are 72 small stupas. Each stupa holds a statue of the Buddha. The film shows the monument as it looks in modern times. It does not show the people who built it.
keyPoints: Borobudur was built in the 700s and 800s in Central Java, Indonesia.
Its levels may follow a Buddhist idea of the universe, from the base to the top.
At the top, 72 small stupas each hold a statue of the Buddha.
watch.contentNote: Not yet watched by a person. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 1 November 2026; the YouTube page itself could not be opened (a bot check), so its length, captions and description were not seen and durationSeconds is null. The summary is based on UNESCO's video archive record of an NHK World Heritage 100 film, "Buddhist Cosmology: Borobudur Temple Compounds" (171 seconds, English), which is probably the same film, and that record's account of the narration; check it against the YouTube video. The film is about the ancient monument, not the 1973–1983 conservation. Preview: by that account the narration mentions Mount Merapi, an active volcano; says the British "rediscovered" Borobudur in 1814 (people in Java knew it was there); and describes a carving of the daughters of "the evil one" trying to tempt the Buddha. UNESCO's record says the film is © NHK, all rights reserved, and re-users must ask NHK's permission: embed the original YouTube player only.

visual.description: A schematic, marked "Schematic", titled "Borobudur, Central Java": four cards joined by arrows. "Ancient monument, 8th–9th century" (plain stepped terraces, no stupas or religious symbols); "Modern conservation, 1973–1983" (the terraces with scaffolding and a worker holding a board); "Records: photos, drawings, film" (a folder with a drawing and a photo, and a film strip); "Future learning: compare, ask why" (a person at a table with two records and a magnifying glass). "Many centuries later" under the gap between the first two cards. The 2017 Memory of the World recognition is in the reading and the timeline, not the diagram.
visual.alt: A diagram of Borobudur in four boxes joined by arrows: the ancient monument from the 8th and 9th centuries, then, many centuries later, modern conservation from 1973 to 1983, then the records made during the work (photos, drawings, film), then future learning, where someone compares the records and asks why.
visual.caption: A modern diagram. It shows how records from repair work help people learn later. It is not a plan of the old building.
visual.lookClosely: Which records would help a future conservator understand a choice?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "International cooperation, Borobudur - UNESCO - PHOTO0000003469 0001.tiff", a black-and-white photo by Gerard Bolla, 1976, from UNESCO's archives, which UNESCO gave to Commons with Wikimedia Sverige. It shows the upper terraces of Borobudur, with metal scaffolding along the left side, rows of small bell-shaped stupas and the large stupa at the top, and part of a tree in the top left corner. Chosen because it is a clearly dated, credited photo of the modern conservation work, so learners can practise separating 1976 from the 700s and 800s. The brief named the companion file ending "0000", which is the typed back of the same print (UNESCO's 1976 caption and the credit "UNESCO/G. Bolla"): use "0001" for the picture. Convert the TIFF to a web JPEG.
secondVisual.alt: A black-and-white photo of Borobudur's upper levels in 1976. Metal scaffolding covers the left side of the carved stone terraces. Rows of small bell-shaped stupas rise to a large stupa at the top.
secondVisual.caption: A real photo of repair work at Borobudur in 1976. It does not show the first building, in the 700s and 800s.
secondVisual.lookClosely: What action is recorded here? What would still need a written record?

sensitiveNotes: Borobudur is a Buddhist place of worship and pilgrimage today. Use respectful, neutral words ("Many Buddhists ...", "UNESCO explains ..."), never rank beliefs, and never ask learners about their own religion; in Speak, "people who come to worship" is a group to think about, not a question about anyone in the room. Preview the video: by UNESCO's account its narration mentions a volcano and describes a carving of the Buddha being tempted.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners keep the ancient monument (built 700s–800s), the 1973–1983 restoration and the 2017 Memory of the World recognition apart, and write an accurate, dated caption with two limits. Evidence move: put the three dates in three boxes on the board before learners look at the 1976 photo. A sound answer gives who (Gerard Bolla for UNESCO), when (1976) and what (modern conservation work), then two questions the photo cannot answer.

Misconception to address: that a conservation photo is evidence of the ancient construction. Source caveats: the archive's numbers (71,851 photo sheets, 6,043 as-built drawing sheets, 425 project documents) come from Indonesia's nomination form on UNESCO's site; the 2017 date comes from news reports of the recognition, as UNESCO's own archive page could not be opened. UNESCO's listing says the temple was rebuilt in two phases in the 1900s, the second from 1973 to 1983; the lesson covers only the second. The back of the 1976 print (Commons file "PHOTO0000003469 0000") carries UNESCO's own typed caption from that time, a source in itself: it calls the work "in progress" and dates UNESCO's agreement with Indonesia to 12 October 1972. Suparno's 2019 exhibition (Borobudur Conservation Office with UNESCO Jakarta) is reported by The Jakarta Post.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.
Followed the brief's checks: what the 1976 photo shows (modern conservation), and record types in the archive, made a choice question (drawings made during the repairs) instead of "name two".

Added to Read part 1, from UNESCO's World Heritage listing: the terraces, carved walls, 72 stupas with Buddha statues, and that the levels follow a Buddhist idea of the universe, so the Watch summary's facts are also in Read.

3A's "former conservation worker and community involvement" (UNESCO's 2019 article): UNESCO's article page could not be opened (a bot check). Used The Jakarta Post's report of the same 2019 exhibition instead: photos by Suparno, Borobudur Conservation Office staff, trained as a photographer to record the restoration. The report says nothing about wider community involvement, so the lesson doesn't claim it.

UNESCO's Memory of the World page for the archive could not be opened (a bot check). The numbers come from Indonesia's nomination form hosted on UNESCO's site (71,851 photo sheets; 6,043 as-built drawing and map sheets) and the 2017 recognition from The Jakarta Post (December 2017) and Antara (via southeastasianarchaeology.com, October 2017). A reviewer should check both on the UNESCO page.

Commons files checked through the Commons API on 1 November 2026. The brief's file ("PHOTO0000003469 0000.tiff") is the typed back of the print, not the photo. The photo is its companion, "PHOTO0000003469 0001.tiff", which I used: Gerard Bolla, 1976, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, attribution "UNESCO / Gerard Bolla", the same as the brief. Alt text written from the photo itself. The back's typed UNESCO caption (1976) is described, in my own words, in the evidence card.
